This model is a LoRA fine-tuned version of `ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-dist-200M`, adapted for **English↔Urdu** translation as part of the **NERDS-NITS** submission to the **WMT 2026 Low-Resource Arabic–Asian Language Translation Shared Task**.

This model forms the **English↔Urdu leg** of the NERDS-NITS pivot-based translation framework:
- For **Arabic→Urdu**, it takes English output from the fine-tuned Arabic→English NLLB-200-600M backbone and translates it into Urdu.
- For **Urdu→Arabic**, it first translates Urdu into English, which is then passed to the fine-tuned English→Arabic NLLB-200-600M backbone to produce the final Arabic translation.

It is the **only IndicTrans2 leg that was fine-tuned** in this submission — the English↔Hindi and English↔Bengali legs used pretrained IndicTrans2-200M checkpoints as-is, without fine-tuning, due to compute constraints.

Direct multilingual translation between Arabic and low-resource Indic languages such as Urdu is constrained by the scarcity of high-quality Arabic–Indic parallel corpora. Since strong dedicated resources exist for both Arabic↔English and English↔Indic translation independently, a pivot architecture was adopted instead of direct fine-tuning. Among the three Indic legs (Hindi, Bengali, Urdu), only the English↔Urdu leg was fine-tuned; the others were left at their pretrained IndicTrans2 checkpoints due to compute constraints.

**Limitations:**
- Trained on a relatively small parallel corpus (~20K sentence pairs); performance may degrade on out-of-domain or highly technical text.
- As one leg of a two-hop translation pipeline (Arabic↔English↔Urdu), errors made by the NLLB-600M backbone can compound with those of this model, particularly under distribution shift.
- LoRA fine-tuning updates only a subset of parameters; performance is bounded by the coverage and biases of the underlying pretrained IndicTrans2-200M checkpoint.
- The paper documents fine-tuning explicitly for the English→Urdu direction; the Urdu→English direction's fine-tuning status should be verified before relying on it as equally fine-tuned.

- **Architecture:** IndicTrans2 distilled 200M-parameter Transformer (English→Indic variant)
- **Fine-tuning strategy:** LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), rank `r = 32`, `α = 64` (α = 2r)
- **Tokenization:** Inherited from the original IndicTrans2-en-indic-dist-200M checkpoint
- **Base model:** `ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-dist-200M`
- **Fine-tuning framework:** Hugging Face `Seq2SeqTrainer`, minimizing sequence-to-sequence cross-entropy loss
- **Task:** English → Urdu machine translation
- **Language codes:** English — `eng_Latn`, Urdu — `urd_Arab`
- **Role in pipeline:** Bridges the pivot pipeline for Arabic↔Urdu translation — the English→Urdu direction feeds Arabic→Urdu (after Arabic→English via NLLB-600M), while the Urdu→English direction feeds Urdu→Arabic (before English→Arabic via NLLB-600M)

> **Note:** the paper explicitly names the fine-tuned `indictrans2-en-indic-dist-200M` (English→Indic) checkpoint for this leg. The corresponding `indic-en` (Urdu→English) checkpoint used for the Urdu→Arabic direction is not separately confirmed as fine-tuned versus pretrained in the paper — treat the Urdu→English direction of this pipeline as unverified until confirmed against your own training logs.

A 200M-parameter translation model finetuned for India Meteorological Department (IMD)
style weather alerts — nowcasts, warnings and advisories for the 38 districts of Bihar —
from English into Hindi (`hin_Deva`), Maithili (`mai_Deva`) and Urdu (`urd_Arab`).

Weather alerts carry numbers (hours, km/h, mm, °C, dates) and place names that must
come through unchanged. This repository therefore ships `imd_translate.py`, which
checks every translation against the English source and marks any output whose numbers
or district names do not match as **not verified**.

This is not an official IMD product.

- **Use for:** English → Indic translation of **casual / conversational** text (chat, dialogue, subtitles).
- **Direction:** English → Indic only. Indic → English / Indic ↔ Indic are untested.
- **Register:** tuned toward casual register; for formal/news text the base model is at least as good.
- **Metric caveat:** improvements are measured by chrF2 and are partly stylistic; **not** human-verified.
- **Low-resource ceiling:** very low-resource languages (e.g. Santali, Sanskrit, Kashmiri) remain
  bounded by the base model's absolute quality.

A conversational/casual-register domain adaptation of
`ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-1B`,
produced with **experience replay** (mixed fine-tuning) + **model souping** (WiSE-FT-style
weight averaging with the base, α=0.6).

> **Scope of the claim — please read.** On the **chrF2** metric, this model **beats
> IndicTrans2-1B on conversational test sets across all 21 Indic languages** (mean **+6.2**,
> paired-bootstrap significant, p ≤ 0.004 on the hardest subtitle tests) while **matching**
> the base on general-domain **FLORES** (mean change −0.17, all within ±0.7 chrF).
> This is a **chrF result**, not a verified human-quality improvement: part of the conversational
> gain plausibly reflects *style-matching* to casual subtitle references rather than better
> adequacy, and a controlled human evaluation has **not** yet confirmed a perceived quality gain.
> Use accordingly. See the paper for the full, honest evaluation and limitations.

These GGUF versions (`f16`, `bf16`, `q8_0`, `tq1_0`, `tq2_0`) were created to optimize the model for efficient inference on resource-constrained environments while preserving translation capabilities.

This model is part of the OPUS-MT project, an effort to make neural machine translation models widely available and accessible for many languages in the world. Indic Translate

---

What is Indic Translate?

**A translation model for English and 22 Indian languages, built for document-length text.**

Indic Translate translates between English and all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule of the
Indian Constitution, in both directions. It is a single-purpose translation model: it
takes one instruction and one piece of source text, and returns the translation. Nothing
else.

Unlike sentence-level MT systems, Indic Translate is designed to take a **whole document in one
request**, up to 32,768 tokens, and return a translation that preserves the document's
paragraph structure, headings, lists, and inline markup.

This release adds three new capabilities: translating directly to and from **Romanized**
script (writing an Indic language with Latin letters, the way people commonly type without
an Indic keyboard), **transliteration**, converting between native and Romanized script
without changing the language, and **code-mixed** translation, to and from text that mixes
English and an Indic language within a sentence.

This model is a LoRA fine-tuned version of `ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-dist-200M`, adapted for **English↔Urdu** translation as part of the **NERDS-NITS** submission to the **WMT 2026 Low-Resource Arabic–Asian Language Translation Shared Task**.

This model forms the **English↔Urdu leg** of the NERDS-NITS pivot-based translation framework:
- For **Arabic→Urdu**, it takes English output from the fine-tuned Arabic→English NLLB-200-600M backbone and translates it into Urdu.
- For **Urdu→Arabic**, it first translates Urdu into English, which is then passed to the fine-tuned English→Arabic NLLB-200-600M backbone to produce the final Arabic translation.

It is the **only IndicTrans2 leg that was fine-tuned** in this submission — the English↔Hindi and English↔Bengali legs used pretrained IndicTrans2-200M checkpoints as-is, without fine-tuning, due to compute constraints.

Direct multilingual translation between Arabic and low-resource Indic languages such as Urdu is constrained by the scarcity of high-quality Arabic–Indic parallel corpora. Since strong dedicated resources exist for both Arabic↔English and English↔Indic translation independently, a pivot architecture was adopted instead of direct fine-tuning. Among the three Indic legs (Hindi, Bengali, Urdu), only the English↔Urdu leg was fine-tuned; the others were left at their pretrained IndicTrans2 checkpoints due to compute constraints.

**Limitations:**
- Trained on a relatively small parallel corpus (~20K sentence pairs); performance may degrade on out-of-domain or highly technical text.
- As one leg of a two-hop translation pipeline (Arabic↔English↔Urdu), errors made by the NLLB-600M backbone can compound with those of this model, particularly under distribution shift.
- LoRA fine-tuning updates only a subset of parameters; performance is bounded by the coverage and biases of the underlying pretrained IndicTrans2-200M checkpoint.
- The paper documents fine-tuning explicitly for the English→Urdu direction; the Urdu→English direction's fine-tuning status should be verified before relying on it as equally fine-tuned.

Fine-tuned on the WMT 2026 Arabic–Urdu-derived English–Urdu parallel data, drawn from the same training split used for the Arabic-Hindi, Arabic-Bangla, and Arabic-Urdu pairs: 20,493 training pairs, with 1,000 dev pairs and 500 devtest pairs.

This model is the **ablation variant** of ayeshasadiq025/nllb-medical-clinical. Both models share the exact same architecture and hyperparameters — **the only difference is the training input**:

| | Baseline (nllb-medical-clinical) | This model (ablation) |
|---|---|---|
| Training input | Raw `english_text` | `masked_english_text` — medical entities replaced with `[MEDICAL_TERM]`, `[DISEASE]`, `[DRUG_CHEMICAL]` tags |
| Architecture | NLLB-200-distilled-600M + LoRA | NLLB-200-distilled-600M + LoRA (identical) |

Result: the baseline (raw text, no masking) outperformed this masked variant — confirming that entity masking hurt translation quality by preventing the model from learning to produce actual Urdu medical terminology.

Use the appropriate target tag (e.g. `tam_Taml`, `ben_Beng`, `mar_Deva`, …) for other languages.

A conversational/casual-register domain adaptation of
`ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-1B`,
produced with **experience replay** (mixed fine-tuning) + **model souping** (WiSE-FT-style
weight averaging with the base, α=0.6).

> **Scope of the claim — please read.** On the **chrF2** metric, this model **beats
> IndicTrans2-1B on conversational test sets across all 21 Indic languages** (mean **+6.2**,
> paired-bootstrap significant, p ≤ 0.004 on the hardest subtitle tests) while **matching**
> the base on general-domain **FLORES** (mean change −0.17, all within ±0.7 chrF).
> This is a **chrF result**, not a verified human-quality improvement: part of the conversational
> gain plausibly reflects *style-matching* to casual subtitle references rather than better
> adequacy, and a controlled human evaluation has **not** yet confirmed a perceived quality gain.
> Use accordingly. See the paper for the full, honest evaluation and limitations.

metadata.text: Translate individual sentences and short text snippets quickly and accurately across **44 language directions**: English ↔ 22 Indian languages.

Indic Translate

---

What is Indic Translate?

**A translation model for English and 22 Indian languages, built for document-length text.**

Indic Translate translates between English and all 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule of the
Indian Constitution, in both directions. It is a single-purpose translation model: it
takes one instruction and one piece of source text, and returns the translation. Nothing
else.

Unlike sentence-level MT systems, Indic Translate is designed to take a **whole document in one
request**, up to 32,768 tokens, and return a translation that preserves the document's
paragraph structure, headings, lists, and inline markup.

This release adds three new capabilities: translating directly to and from **Romanized**
script (writing an Indic language with Latin letters, the way people commonly type without
an Indic keyboard), **transliteration**, converting between native and Romanized script
without changing the language, and **code-mixed** translation, to and from text that mixes
English and an Indic language within a sentence.
